learnings.title: The layered frontend architecture — the sketch to start from
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Every frontend design round asks you to draw something in the first ten minutes. Having one reference sketch in your head — and knowing which boxes to *delete* for the problem in front of you — is worth more than any individual technology.

## The sketch

![The layered frontend architecture](/diagrams/sysdesign/architecture-layers.svg)

## Walking it, out loud

The diagram is only half the answer. The other half is saying what each box **owns**, because a box with no stated responsibility is decoration.

### App shell

The only code that is always loaded. It owns routing, the auth session, page layout, and the top-level error boundaries. Everything else is lazy.

> "The shell is the thing I can't code-split, so it's the thing I keep small. Routing, session, layout, error boundaries — and nothing else."

### Feature modules

One per product area, lazily loaded, **one owner each**. The ownership half matters as much as the technical half: modules are how you give three teams somewhere to work without colliding.

### Design system

Tokens, primitives, components. Its real job is not consistency — it is that accessibility and theming get solved once instead of once per team.

### Data layer

The server cache, request deduplication, and mutations. Deliberately separate from UI state, because server data is a *copy* of something someone else owns and needs staleness and refetch policies that plain application state does not.

### Platform

Service worker (offline shell and asset caching), IndexedDB (local data), Web Workers (anything expensive that must not block rendering).

### And underneath all of it: one main thread

The single most important constraint in the diagram. Rendering, your JavaScript, and input handling all share it. Everything above competes for the same ~10 ms per frame — which is why "just do it on the client" is never free.

## Deleting boxes is the skill

The sketch is a starting point, not a template. Saying which parts you are *not* building, and why, is a stronger signal than drawing all of them:

| Problem | What you delete |
| --- | --- |
| Internal admin tool | CDN strategy, SSR, offline, i18n — it is behind a VPN on good laptops |
| Marketing site | Data layer, most state management — it is static content |
| Offline-first field app | Nothing; the platform row becomes the centre of the design |
| Single-team MVP | Feature modules, design system — one app, five shared components |
| Embedded partner widget | The shell — you are living inside someone else's page, which changes everything |

> "For an internal dashboard I'd draw this and then cross out the CDN layer, SSR, and the offline story. It's behind a login on company laptops — I'd rather spend the complexity budget on the data layer, because that's where the actual problem is."

## The order to draw it in

1. **The client box first**, and say "one device, one main thread". It frames every later trade-off.
2. **The network path second** — what is between the user and the data, and how many hops.
3. **Cross-cutting last**, briefly — observability, i18n, flags, security — so they are on the board and you can return to any of them in the optimisations stage.

Drawing cross-cutting concerns early and then never mentioning them again is worse than not drawing them; it looks like a memorised template.

## Common mistakes

- **Boxes with no responsibility.** "State management" as a box says nothing. "Server cache with a 30 s stale window" says something.
- **Drawing all of it every time.** A template recited is not a design.
- **Omitting the main thread.** It is the constraint that makes this a frontend problem at all.
- **Cross-cutting concerns as set dressing.** If you draw it, be ready to go deep on it.

## Key takeaways

- One reference sketch: shell, feature modules, design system, data layer, platform — over one main thread.
- Name what each box owns; an unowned box is decoration.
- Deleting boxes for the problem at hand is the actual signal.
- Draw client, then network path, then cross-cutting.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Which box would you build first?"** — The shell and one feature module end to end. A thin vertical slice beats a broad skeleton.
- **"What if the team is one person?"** — Delete the feature-module boundary and the design system. Both are coordination tools, and there is nothing to coordinate.
- **"Where does the complexity actually live?"** — Almost always the data layer and the boundary between the client and the network. Say so and go there.

learnings.title: Rendering strategies — CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming, islands
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
"Where does the HTML come from?" is the first architectural decision in any frontend design, and every later decision — caching, state, data fetching, bundle strategy — inherits from it. ## The picture ![Rendering strategies compared on one timeline](/diagrams/sysdesign/rendering-strategies.svg) Read the diagram carefully, because it contains the insight most candidates miss: **all four strategies ship the same JavaScript, so they all reach interactive at roughly the same moment.** What you are choosing is how early something is *readable*, and what you pay for that. ## The five ### CSR — Client-Side Rendering The server sends an empty shell; the browser downloads JS, fetches data, and renders. - **Good:** trivial to host (a bucket and a CDN), no server runtime, simple mental model - **Bad:** the slowest possible first paint — nothing until JS *and* data have landed - **Use when:** behind a login, where SEO is irrelevant and the user is already waiting — dashboards, admin tools, editors ### SSR — Server-Side Rendering The server fetches data and renders HTML per request. - **Good:** fast, complete first paint; SEO works; personalisation is possible - **Bad:** a server per request, so it costs money and can fall over; TTFB now includes your data fetch - **Use when:** content is personalised *and* must be indexed or paint fast — feeds, product pages with stock and pricing ### SSG — Static Site Generation Rendered once at build time, served as files from a CDN. - **Good:** the fastest possible paint; effectively free; nothing to fall over - **Bad:** content is as old as your last build; a large site has a long build - **Use when:** content changes rarely and is the same for everyone — docs, marketing, blogs ### ISR — Incremental Static Regeneration SSG plus a revalidation window: serve the cached page, regenerate in the background when stale. - **Good:** static speed with bounded staleness; no full rebuild - **Bad:** the first visitor after expiry may see stale content; needs a platform that supports it - **Use when:** a large catalogue that changes but not per-user — e-commerce listings, news ### Streaming SSR + islands Send the shell immediately, stream slow sections as they resolve, and hydrate only the interactive parts. - **Good:** early paint *and* early interactivity; slow data no longer blocks the whole page - **Bad:** the most complex to reason about and debug; needs framework support - **Use when:** the page has one slow section and a lot of static content around it ## Choosing, out loud ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Does it need SEO or a fast
first paint for a new visitor?"] -->|No| CSR["CSR — ship a shell"] A -->|Yes| B["Is the content the same
for every user?"] B -->|Yes| C["Does it change often?"] C -->|Rarely| SSG["SSG"] C -->|Often| ISR["ISR"] B -->|No, personalised| D["Is one section much
slower than the rest?"] D -->|No| SSR["SSR"] D -->|Yes| ST["Streaming SSR + islands"] ``` ## The trap: hydration SSR is often described as "fast". It is fast to *paint* and no faster to become *interactive* — and the gap between those is dangerous, because the page looks ready and does not respond. > **The uncanny valley of SSR:** the button is on screen at 400 ms and does nothing until 1400 ms. A user who clicks in that second gets no feedback at all, and their input may be lost entirely. Mitigations, in order of impact: 1. **Ship less JS** — the only real fix; hydration cost is proportional to it 2. **Islands / partial hydration** — hydrate the three interactive components, not the whole tree 3. **Progressive hydration** — hydrate on interaction or when visible 4. **Design for it** — disable controls until hydrated rather than letting clicks vanish ## Mixing per route The choice is per route, not per app, and saying so lands well: | Route | Strategy | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | `/` marketing | SSG | Same for everyone, changes weekly | | `/products/:id` | ISR, 60s | Large catalogue, prices move | | `/feed` | Streaming SSR | Personalised, ranking is the slow part | | `/settings` | CSR | Behind auth, no SEO, already engaged | > "I'd treat this per route rather than picking one for the app. The marketing pages are static, the catalogue is ISR on a 60-second window, and only the feed actually needs per-request rendering — which also means only the feed needs the server capacity." ## Common mistakes - **"SSR is faster" with no qualifier.** Faster to paint, not to interactive. - **One strategy for the whole app.** Routes have different needs; frameworks support mixing. - **SSR without measuring TTFB.** You moved the data fetch onto the critical path; if the API is slow, SSR is now *slower* than CSR. - **Ignoring hydration entirely.** It is often the largest single cost in the whole load. ## Key takeaways - All strategies ship the same JS, so they converge on interactive; they differ on when content is readable and what that costs. - CSR for authenticated tools, SSG for static content, ISR for big catalogues, SSR for personalised, streaming when one section is slow. - Choose per route, not per app. - Hydration is the hidden cost — the fix is shipping less JS, then islands. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How would you pick between SSR and SSG here?"** — Ask whether the content is per-user and how stale it may be. Those two answers decide it. - **"What if TTFB got worse after moving to SSR?"** — Expected: you put the data fetch on the critical path. Cache at the edge, or stream the shell before the data resolves. - **"How do you know hydration is the problem?"** — A large gap between FCP and INP-eligible interactivity, plus long tasks clustered right after load.

learnings.title: API design for frontends — REST, GraphQL, tRPC and the BFF
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
"That's the backend's job" is a failing answer. The API contract is the single boundary that decides how many round trips your screen costs, how much data you ship, and how coupled your UI is to someone else's data model. ## The problem every option is solving A product page needs: the product, its stock level, its reviews, and whether *this* user has it in their cart. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph N["Naive REST — 4 sequential round trips"] A1["GET /products/42"] --> A2["GET /products/42/stock"] A2 --> A3["GET /products/42/reviews"] A3 --> A4["GET /me/cart"] end ``` On 4G that is four × ~100 ms of latency before the page is complete — and the waterfall is sequential because each request needs the previous response's ids. **The API shape has just cost you 400 ms that no amount of frontend optimisation can recover.** ## The four answers ### REST Resource-oriented, cacheable, universally understood. - **Good:** HTTP caching works out of the box; every tool understands it; easy to reason about - **Bad:** over-fetching (the full product when you needed the title), under-fetching (the N+1 waterfall above) - **Mitigations that keep it viable:** compound endpoints (`/products/42?include=stock,reviews`), sparse fieldsets (`?fields=id,title,price`), and `HTTP/2` so parallel requests are cheap ### GraphQL One endpoint; the client declares the shape it wants. ```graphql query ProductPage($id: ID!) { product(id: $id) { title price stock { available } reviews(first: 5) { nodes { rating body } } } me { cart { contains(productId: $id) } } } ``` - **Good:** one round trip, exactly the fields needed, a typed schema, strong tooling - **Bad:** HTTP caching does not apply (everything is a POST to one URL), so you now own caching in the client; query cost and depth need server-side limits; the client bundle grows ### tRPC Typed RPC where client and server share TypeScript types directly. - **Good:** end-to-end type safety with no codegen step; almost no runtime overhead - **Bad:** requires a TypeScript backend you control — unusable across an org boundary or for a public API ### BFF — Backend For Frontend A thin service owned by the frontend team that composes downstream calls into exactly what a screen needs. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Client
1 request"] --> B["BFF"] B --> P["product-service"] B --> S["inventory-service"] B --> R["review-service"] B --> U["cart-service"] B --> C ``` - **Good:** one round trip; the joins happen on fast internal links instead of the user's 4G; the client is decoupled from the microservice layout; you can cache, batch, and reshape freely - **Bad:** a service to own, deploy and monitor; a new place for bugs; another team boundary if you do not own it ## Choosing | Situation | Reach for | | --- | --- | | Public API, many unknown consumers | REST | | One team, TypeScript on both sides | tRPC | | Many clients with genuinely different data needs (web, iOS, Android, watch) | GraphQL | | Microservices behind you and one screen needs four of them | BFF | | Mobile-first with a tight latency budget | BFF or GraphQL — round trips are the enemy | > "I'd put a BFF in front. The screen needs four services, and doing that join over the user's 4G connection costs 400 ms that a 5 ms internal join doesn't. It also means the client never learns the microservice layout, which is the part most likely to be reorganised." ## Contract decisions that matter more than the protocol ### Pagination — cursor, not offset ```javascript // Offset: on a feed that mutates, page 2 duplicates and skips items. GET /feed?offset=20&limit=20 // Cursor: stable under insertion; the only correct choice for a live list. GET /feed?cursor=eyJpZCI6MTIzfQ&limit=20 → { items: [...], nextCursor: 'eyJpZCI6MTQzfQ' | null } ``` Offset is fine for stable, page-numbered data — an admin table. It is *incorrect* for anything that mutates while you read it. ### A consistent error shape ```javascript { error: { code: 'RATE_LIMITED', // stable, switchable in code message: 'Too many requests', // human-readable, loggable retryAfter: 30, // actionable fields: { email: 'Already registered' }, // for form errors } } ``` Without a `code`, the client ends up matching on English message text, which breaks the first time someone improves the copy or ships a translation. ### Idempotency for mutations ```javascript POST /orders Idempotency-Key: 8f3a-2b91-... // generated once per user intent ``` Any mutation the client might retry — and every mutation over a flaky mobile network is a mutation the client might retry — needs this, or a dropped response becomes a double charge. ## Common mistakes - **Accepting whatever the backend offers.** Design the contract from what the screen needs, backwards. - **Offset pagination on a live feed.** A correctness bug, not a style preference. - **GraphQL "because it's modern".** You have traded HTTP caching for client complexity; make sure you needed the trade. - **Error messages with no code.** Guarantees string-matching in the client. - **No idempotency key on payments.** The classic double-charge. ## Key takeaways - The API shape decides your round trips, and round trips dominate your latency budget. - REST for public and cacheable, GraphQL for many divergent clients, tRPC for one TypeScript team, BFF when a screen needs several services. - A BFF moves the join off the user's network onto an internal one. - Cursor pagination, a coded error shape, and idempotency keys matter more than which protocol you picked. ## Interview follow-ups - **"The backend says they can't change the endpoints."** — That is the BFF argument, made for you. Price it: one small service versus a permanent latency tax on every screen. - **"How do you cache GraphQL?"** — Not with HTTP. Normalised client cache keyed by entity id, plus persisted queries if you want edge caching back. - **"Why is cursor pagination better?"** — Not neater — *correct*. Offset duplicates and skips when the underlying list mutates between pages.

learnings.title: Data fetching and the five caching layers
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Almost every frontend performance question eventually becomes a caching question. The mistake is answering "I'd cache it" — every layer below caches, and each one goes stale in its own way. ## The layers ![The five caches a request falls through](/diagrams/sysdesign/caching-layers.svg) A request falls through these top to bottom and stops at the first one that answers. The cost of each layer is not the lookup — it is **who is responsible for invalidating it**. ## Layer by layer ### 1. In-memory (React Query / SWR / RTK Query) The cache your application code actually talks to. ```javascript useQuery({ queryKey: ['feed', cursor], queryFn: fetchFeed, staleTime: 30_000, // trusted without asking for 30s gcTime: 5 * 60_000, // kept in memory 5 min after nothing uses it }); ``` `staleTime` is the one that matters and the one people leave at its default of `0`, which means every mount refetches. Set it to how long the data is *actually* good for. This layer buys you request deduplication for free: three components asking for the same key produce one request. ### 2. Service worker (Cache Storage) Programmable, survives reload, and the only layer that works with no network at all. ```javascript // Stale-while-revalidate: answer instantly, refresh in the background. self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => { if (!event.request.url.includes('/api/')) return; event.respondWith( caches.open('api-v1').then(async (cache) => { const cached = await cache.match(event.request); const fresh = fetch(event.request).then((res) => { cache.put(event.request, res.clone()); return res; }); return cached ?? fresh; // cached wins the race when present }), ); }); ``` The power and the danger are the same thing: **nothing evicts this but your own code.** A service worker with a bug is installed on the user's device until you explicitly replace it. Ship the kill switch before you ship the caching. ### 3. HTTP cache The browser's own disk cache, driven entirely by response headers. | Header | Meaning | Use for | | --- | --- | --- | | `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` | Never revalidate | Hashed assets — `app.8f3a2b.js` | | `Cache-Control: no-cache` | Store it, but revalidate every time | HTML | | `Cache-Control: private, max-age=60` | 60s, browser only, never a shared cache | Personalised JSON | | `ETag` + `If-None-Match` | Revalidate cheaply, 304 with no body | Anything large that rarely changes | **The rule that prevents the worst outage:** hash your assets and cache them forever; never cache the HTML. Invert those two and your next deploy reaches nobody, with no way to push a fix. ### 4. CDN edge Shared across every user near that point of presence. ``` Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600 ``` That says: the edge may serve this for 60 seconds without asking; for the following 10 minutes it may still serve the stale copy *while* it fetches a fresh one in the background. Almost every user gets an edge-speed response, and only the revalidation pays origin latency. **The catastrophic mistake at this layer** is caching a personalised response publicly. One user's data is now served to everyone near that POP. Anything user-specific is `private`, or is split out of the cacheable response entirely. ### 5. Origin The truth. Everything above exists so you reach this rarely. ## Splitting the response — the trick worth knowing Personalisation is what makes a response uncacheable. So do not personalise the whole response: ```mermaid flowchart LR R["GET /feed"] --> S["Shell + ranked post ids
public, s-maxage=60
→ served by the CDN"] R --> P["/me/overlay: my likes,
my unread, my saved
private, no-store
→ origin, but tiny"] ``` > "The ranked list is the same for everyone in a cohort, so it can sit at the edge for a minute. What's personal is which of those posts I've liked — that's a tiny separate call. One uncacheable 250 ms request becomes a 30 ms edge hit plus an 80 ms overlay, and the overlay can arrive after first paint." ## Invalidation strategies | Strategy | How | Good for | | --- | --- | --- | | **TTL** | `max-age` and wait | Content with a tolerable staleness window | | **Revalidation** | `ETag` / `Last-Modified` | Large, rarely-changing responses | | **Purge on write** | Call the CDN purge API when content is published | Editorial content, low write volume | | **Cache keys with versions** | `/v3/config.json` | Config, feature flags | | **Content hashing** | `app.8f3a2b.js` | All static assets — the only true solution | ## Common mistakes - **"I'd cache it"** with no layer and no invalidation named. This is the single most common weak answer in the round. - **Caching HTML immutably.** Your deploy never lands and you cannot push a fix. - **Personalised data in a public cache.** A real, reportable data leak. - **`staleTime: 0`.** Every mount refetches and the client cache does nothing. - **A service worker shipped before its update path.** You cannot recall it. ## Key takeaways - Name the layer *and* the invalidation together — that pairing is the whole answer. - Hash assets and cache forever; never cache HTML. - `stale-while-revalidate` at the edge gives almost everyone an edge-speed response. - Split responses so the cacheable part can be public and only the tiny personal part hits the origin. - The service worker is the only layer whose bugs you cannot evict remotely. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How do you invalidate after a publish?"** — Purge API for the edge, content hash for assets, and a query-key invalidation for the in-memory layer. All three, or it is stale somewhere. - **"What if the CDN serves stale data after a price change?"** — Either shorten `s-maxage` or purge on write. Then say which you would pick and why — purge costs coupling, TTL costs staleness. - **"How would you cache a search results page?"** — Ask whether results are personalised. If ranked per user, the edge is out and you are caching per-session in memory.

learnings.title: State topology — the four kinds and where each one lives
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
"How would you manage state?" is not a question about libraries. It is a question about whether you can tell four different kinds of state apart — because almost every state management disaster is one kind living in the wrong place.

## The four kinds

![Four kinds of state and where each one lives](/diagrams/sysdesign/state-topology.svg)

## The classification test

For any piece of state, ask in this order:

1. **Does it live on a server and could someone else change it?** → **server cache**
2. **Should a refresh or a shared link restore it?** → **URL**
3. **Is it an uncommitted edit that would be annoying to lose?** → **form / draft state**
4. **Otherwise** → **local UI state**, as close to the element as possible

Running this out loud during the interview is worth more than naming any library:

> "Let me classify the state first. The posts are a server cache — someone else can like them while I'm looking. The active filter belongs in the URL, because people share filtered views. The comment I'm half-typing is draft state and should survive a reload. Whether the emoji picker is open is local UI state and belongs in that component. Only the first one needs a data-fetching library."

## Why server cache is not "global state"

This is the confusion that produces 3,000-line reducers. Server data is not state you own — it is a **copy of state someone else owns**, and copies have properties application state does not:

| Server cache needs | Global state has |
| --- | --- |
| Staleness — when should I distrust this? | Nothing |
| Refetch triggers — mount, focus, reconnect, mutation | Nothing |
| Deduplication — three components, one request | Nothing |
| Background refresh | Nothing |
| Per-key loading and error states | One giant `isLoading` |

Hand-rolling all of that in a reducer is how teams end up with a state layer nobody wants to touch. `React Query`, `SWR` and `RTK Query` exist because this is a solved problem with a lot of edge cases.

## The URL is state, and it is free

Filters, tabs, pagination, sort order, the open item in a master–detail view — all of it belongs in the URL:

```javascript
const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();
const status = params.get('status') ?? 'all';

// Replace, don't push — a filter change shouldn't require five
// back presses to escape.
setParams((prev) => {
  prev.set('status', next);
  return prev;
}, { replace: true });
```

You get for free: shareable links, working back button, restore on refresh, and bookmarkable views. Putting this in a store and then building "copy link to this view" by hand is doing the same work twice, worse.

## Normalised or nested?

A real data-model decision, not a preference:

```javascript
// Nested — matches the API response, easy to render
{ feed: [{ id: 'p1', author: { id: 'u9', name: 'Ada' }, likes: 12 }] }

// Normalised — one copy of each entity, lists hold ids
{
  posts: { p1: { id: 'p1', authorId: 'u9', likes: 12 } },
  users: { u9: { id: 'u9', name: 'Ada' } },
  feed:  { ids: ['p1'], cursor: '…' },
}
```

**Normalise when the same entity appears in more than one place** — a post in the feed, in search results, and on its own page. Liking it once should update all three. With a nested shape you have three copies and two of them are now wrong.

**Do not normalise** a simple list rendered in exactly one place. You have added a join for no benefit.

## Choosing a library, priced

| Need | Reach for | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server data | React Query / SWR / RTK Query | A concept to learn; almost always worth it |
| URL state | The router | None |
| Form state | React Hook Form / TanStack Form | Small |
| A little shared UI state | Context + `useState` | Re-renders every consumer — keep it small and split by concern |
| A lot of shared UI state, fine-grained | Zustand / Jotai | A dependency, minimal API |
| Complex state machines | XState | Real learning curve; earns it for wizards, players, editors |
| Large app, time-travel debugging, strict conventions | Redux Toolkit | Boilerplate, and often used for things RTK Query should own |

> "I'd reach for React Query plus the URL, and only add Zustand if there's genuinely shared UI state across distant parts of the tree. I'd expect that to be a handful of values — theme, the command palette, maybe a global toast queue."

## Common mistakes

- **One store for all four kinds.** Stale server data, unshareable filters, and a modal that re-renders the app.
- **Context for high-frequency state.** Every consumer re-renders on every change. Fine for theme; wrong for cursor position.
- **Filters in a store.** You have just deleted shareable links and the back button.
- **Over-normalising.** A join you maintain by hand for a list rendered once.
- **Naming a library before classifying the state.** It reveals the order you think in.

## Key takeaways

- Four kinds: server cache, URL, form/draft, local UI — and the classification comes before the library.
- Server data is a copy of someone else's state and needs staleness, refetching and dedup, which a plain store does not give you.
- The URL gives you sharing, back, and restore for free.
- Normalise only when an entity is rendered in more than one place.
- Keep local state local; distance from the element is the cost.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Would you use Redux here?"** — Ask what for. If the answer is server data, RTK Query is the right part of Redux. If it is UI state in three places, Context or Zustand is smaller.
- **"How do two components share a filter?"** — The URL. Then they are not sharing state at all, they are both reading the same address.
- **"What happens when a like is made on the detail page?"** — With a normalised cache, invalidate the entity and every list showing it is correct. That is the argument for normalising.

learnings.title: Offline-first and background sync
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Offline is not a feature you add. It is a decision about whether your app's source of truth is the network or the device — and that decision reaches into every mutation you write. ## The four levels Ask which one is actually required before designing anything. They differ by an order of magnitude in cost. | Level | Behaviour | Cost | | --- | --- | --- | | **0 — Online only** | Network error, nothing works | Free | | **1 — Graceful** | Show cached data read-only, tell the user they are offline | Small | | **2 — Offline reads** | The app fully works for reading, from a local store | Medium | | **3 — Offline writes** | Create and edit offline, sync and resolve conflicts later | Large | > "Which level do you need? Level 1 is almost free and I'd do it regardless. Level 3 turns every mutation into a queued, idempotent, conflict-resolvable operation — that's most of the design, so I want to be sure it's a requirement before I build it." ## The pieces ```mermaid flowchart TD UI["UI"] --> L["Local store
(IndexedDB)"] UI --> Q["Outbox
(pending mutations)"] L --> UI Q --> S["Sync engine"] S -->|"online"| API["Server"] API --> M["Merge + conflict resolution"] M --> L SW["Service worker
(shell + assets)"] --> UI ``` The shape that makes offline work is inverting the flow: **the UI reads and writes to the local store, and a separate sync engine reconciles it with the server.** As long as the UI awaits the network, you do not have an offline app — you have an online app with a nice error message. ### The service worker handles the shell ```javascript // Assets: cache-first, because they are content-hashed and immutable. // Navigations: network-first with a cached fallback, so a deploy lands. self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => { const { request } = event; if (request.mode === 'navigate') { event.respondWith( fetch(request).catch(() => caches.match('/offline.html')), ); return; } if (request.destination === 'script' || request.destination === 'style') { event.respondWith( caches.match(request).then((hit) => hit ?? fetch(request)), ); } }); ``` ### IndexedDB holds the data Not `localStorage` — it is synchronous (so it blocks the main thread), string-only, and capped around 5 MB. IndexedDB is async, structured, and measured in hundreds of megabytes. Use a wrapper (`idb`, `Dexie`); the raw API is genuinely unpleasant. ### The outbox holds intent ```javascript // Record the INTENT, not the resulting state. await outbox.add({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), // doubles as the idempotency key op: 'comment.create', payload: { threadId, body }, baseVersion: thread.version, // what we believed when we acted createdAt: Date.now(), }); ``` Storing intent rather than final state is what makes conflict resolution possible. "Append this comment" can be replayed onto a changed thread; "the thread is now exactly this" cannot. ## Conflict resolution When you sync, the server may have moved on. There are exactly four strategies: | Strategy | How it behaves | Right for | | --- | --- | --- | | **Last write wins** | Newest timestamp overwrites | Low-stakes, single-user-ish data — a draft, a setting | | **Server wins** | Discard the local change | Data the client should not own — pricing, permissions | | **Merge by operation** | Replay intents onto the new state | Appends and counters — comments, likes | | **CRDT** | Data structures that converge by construction | Genuine concurrent editing | The honest answer to "how do you handle conflicts" is usually: **per field, not per record.** > "Last-write-wins on the document title is fine. On the body of a collaboratively edited document it silently destroys someone's work — that field needs operational merge or a CRDT. I'd pick per field rather than per record." And when you genuinely cannot merge, **ask**. A conflict UI that shows both versions is a legitimate design, and often the honest one. ## Making it feel instant Offline-first has a pleasant side effect: since the UI reads from a local store, it is fast even when online. ```javascript async function addComment(body) { const optimistic = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), body, pending: true }; await local.comments.put(optimistic); // UI updates immediately await outbox.add({ op: 'comment.create', payload: optimistic }); sync(); // fire and forget } ``` Render `pending: true` items in a subdued state so the user can tell what has landed and what has not. Hiding the distinction is what makes users distrust an app after one failed sync. ## Background Sync ```javascript const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready; await reg.sync.register('outbox-flush'); // fires when connectivity returns ``` Chromium-only, so it is an enhancement, not a foundation. Always also flush on `online` and on app start. ## Common mistakes - **`localStorage` for app data.** Synchronous, tiny, string-only. - **Queuing final state instead of intent.** Makes merging impossible. - **No idempotency key.** Every retry creates a duplicate. - **Hiding pending state.** The user cannot tell what is saved. - **Last-write-wins on collaborative text.** Silent, unrecoverable data loss. - **Unbounded local storage.** Eviction, quota errors, and a phone with no space. ## Key takeaways - Pick the level deliberately; level 3 is most of an architecture and level 1 is nearly free. - Offline works only when the UI reads and writes locally and a sync engine reconciles. - IndexedDB for data, service worker for the shell, an outbox for intent. - Queue intent, not state, and attach an idempotency key to every entry. - Resolve conflicts per field, and show a conflict UI when a merge would destroy work. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Two devices edited the same record offline."** — Name the field. Title: last-write-wins. Comment list: merge appends. Body text: CRDT or ask the user. - **"How do you stop duplicates on retry?"** — Client-generated idempotency key, stored with the outbox entry so a retry reuses it. - **"How much can you store?"** — Hundreds of MB typically, but it is evictable. Design for the quota error and for the data disappearing.

learnings.title: Micro-frontends — the deploy problem, and its price
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Micro-frontends solve exactly one problem: **independent deployment for independent teams.** Every other reason people give — "modularity", "technology freedom", "smaller bundles" — is either achievable more cheaply or is actually a downside in disguise. Knowing the price is what makes this a senior topic. ## The actual problem ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph M["Monolith: one deploy"] T1["Team A"] --> R["shared repo"] T2["Team B"] --> R T3["Team C"] --> R R --> D["One pipeline
One team's red test
blocks everyone"] end ``` With three teams this is a mild annoyance. With twelve, a release train becomes a standing meeting, and the slowest team sets everyone's cadence. *That* is the pain micro-frontends address. If your release pain is not this specific pain, they will not help. ## The three ways to do it ### Build-time composition (npm packages) Each team publishes a package; the shell depends on them. - **Good:** simple, one bundle, one runtime, no new infrastructure - **Bad:** **not actually independent deployment** — shipping a change still means bumping a version and redeploying the shell - **Verdict:** good modularity, does not solve the deploy problem ### Run-time composition — Module Federation Webpack/Rspack loads remote bundles at runtime. ```javascript // shell new ModuleFederationPlugin({ remotes: { checkout: 'checkout@https://cdn.example.com/checkout/remote.js' }, shared: { react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^19.0.0' }, 'react-dom': { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^19.0.0' }, }, }); ``` - **Good:** genuinely independent deploys; shared dependencies loaded once - **Bad:** a version mismatch is now a **runtime** failure in production rather than a build failure in CI; debugging crosses bundle boundaries; `singleton: true` on React is mandatory and quietly couples every team's upgrade schedule ### iframes - **Good:** real isolation — separate CSS, separate JS, separate crashes; the only option when embedding third-party or legacy apps - **Bad:** routing, auth, resizing, focus and accessibility all become manual; every shared interaction is `postMessage`; the UX seams are visible ## The bill Be able to recite this. It is what separates an opinion from a decision: | You must build and own | Why it is not free | | --- | --- | | **A shell** | Routing, auth, layout, error isolation — a real product with an owner | | **A design system** | Without one, users see three different button styles on one page | | **A shared dependency policy** | React as a singleton means everyone upgrades together, which is the coupling you were escaping | | **Cross-app contracts** | Events, shared state, and a versioning policy for both | | **Distributed debugging** | A stack trace now crosses teams and bundles | | **Performance governance** | Every team ships their own bundle; without budgets the total only grows | | **Integration testing** | Individually green, together broken, is the characteristic failure | > "Realistically it's a shell team — one or two engineers permanently — plus a design system, plus a dependency policy. Under about five or six frontend teams, I'd stay in a monorepo with enforced ownership boundaries and get most of the modularity for a fraction of that." ## The cheaper alternatives, in order Try these first, and say so: 1. **Monorepo with `CODEOWNERS`** — ownership boundaries without runtime cost 2. **Route-level code splitting** — the bundle benefit with none of the complexity 3. **Trunk-based development with feature flags** — decouples *release* from *deploy*, which is the actual goal 4. **Independent pipelines per package** — parallel CI without runtime federation 5. **Then**, if deploy coordination is still the measured bottleneck, micro-frontends Step 3 deserves emphasis: **feature flags give you independent release without independent deployment**, and that is what most teams actually wanted. ## When it is genuinely right - Six or more frontend teams with distinct release cadences - A legacy app being strangled incrementally (the strangler fig pattern — one of the strongest cases) - Embedding a genuinely third-party application - Acquisitions on different stacks that must appear as one product ## Common mistakes - **Adopting them for modularity.** A monorepo gives you that free. - **"Technology freedom."** Three frameworks on one page means three runtimes downloaded and a design system that cannot exist. - **Claiming smaller bundles.** Usually larger — duplicated dependencies, plus federation runtime. - **No design system first.** The most visible failure: one page, three visual languages. - **Not pricing the shell.** It is a product, and it needs an owner. ## Key takeaways - The one problem they solve is independent deployment for independent teams. - Build-time composition gives modularity but not independent deploys; Module Federation gives deploys and turns version mismatches into production failures. - The price is a shell team, a design system, a dependency policy, and cross-boundary debugging. - Feature flags decouple release from deploy far more cheaply, and that is usually the real requirement. - Under five or six teams, a monorepo with ownership boundaries wins. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How do two micro-frontends share state?"** — Ideally they do not. If they must: a URL, a narrow event contract, or a shell-owned store — and now you have a versioned contract to maintain. - **"How do you keep them visually consistent?"** — A versioned design system, and it must exist *before* the split, not after. - **"How do you stop the bundle exploding?"** — Shared singletons plus a per-remote size budget enforced in each team's CI.

learnings.title: Design systems as architecture, not decoration
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
A design system is usually presented as a visual consistency project. In a system design interview it is better framed as what it actually is: **the mechanism that makes accessibility, theming, and cross-team consistency solvable once instead of per feature.** ## The layers ```mermaid flowchart TD T["Design tokens
colour, space, type, radius, motion"] --> P["Primitives
Box, Stack, Text, Icon"] P --> C["Components
Button, Input, Modal, Table"] C --> Pat["Patterns
form layouts, empty states, page shells"] Pat --> F["Features"] ``` Each layer may only depend downward. A `Button` that imports something from a feature is the bug that turns a design system into a second application. ### Tokens are the contract ```css :root { /* Primitive — raw values, never used directly in a component */ --blue-600: #2563eb; --gray-900: #111827; --space-4: 16px; /* Semantic — what components actually reference */ --color-action: var(--blue-600); --color-text: var(--gray-900); --space-inset: var(--space-4); } [data-theme='dark'] { --color-action: var(--blue-400); --color-text: var(--gray-50); } ``` The two-layer split is the whole trick. Components reference `--color-action`; nothing references `--blue-600`. **Dark mode, white-labelling and a rebrand all become a change to the semantic layer** — no component is touched. A component with a raw hex in it is a component that cannot be themed, and that is why "never a raw hex in a component rule" is a rule worth enforcing in lint. ## Where the real value is ### Accessibility, solved once The strongest argument, and the one candidates skip: > "If every team builds its own modal, every team gets focus trapping, restoring focus on close, `Escape` handling, `aria-modal`, and scroll locking wrong in a slightly different way. One audited `Modal` in the design system means you fix it once and 40 usages get it." This applies to every component with real behaviour: menus, comboboxes, tabs, tooltips, date pickers. It is the difference between accessibility as an ongoing tax and accessibility as a one-time investment. ### Headless where behaviour is hard For anything with complex interaction, split behaviour from appearance: ```javascript // Behaviour from a headless library (Radix, React Aria, Headless UI): // keyboard, focus, ARIA, collision detection — the parts that take // months to get right. // Appearance from your tokens. … ``` > "I wouldn't hand-roll a combobox. The ARIA pattern alone is a week, and then there's typeahead, virtual focus, and collision detection. I'd take a headless library for behaviour and own only the styling." ## The API design that decides adoption A design system fails when teams fork it, and teams fork it when it will not bend. The fix is a deliberate escape hatch policy: | Approach | Effect | | --- | --- | | **Closed** — a fixed prop list | Consistent, and forked the first time someone needs something you did not anticipate | | **Open** — `className` and `style` pass through | Flexible, and consistency erodes quietly | | **Compound** — ``, `` | Composable where it matters, opinionated where it should be. **Usually right.** | | **Variants** — `variant="danger" size="sm"` | Constrained flexibility; pairs well with compound | Give teams a documented way out — a `Slot`/`asChild` prop, or a lower-level primitive — so that "it doesn't do what I need" produces a pull request instead of a copy-paste. ## Versioning and migration This is what makes it an architecture question: - **Semver, seriously.** A visual change that breaks a layout is a breaking change even if the types did not move. - **Deprecate before removing.** Warn in dev for at least one minor version. - **Ship codemods for breaking changes.** Migrating 200 call sites by hand is how a version becomes permanently stranded. - **Visual regression tests** — Chromatic, Percy, or Playwright screenshots. Unit tests do not catch a 4 px padding change across 60 components. - **A living usage dashboard.** You cannot deprecate what you cannot find. ## Common mistakes - **Raw values in components.** Nothing can be themed afterwards. - **Wrapping every HTML element.** `
` adds nothing but a dependency. - **No escape hatch.** Guarantees forks, and forks are worse than flexibility. - **Hand-rolling complex ARIA.** Comboboxes and date pickers are where headless libraries pay for themselves. - **No visual regression testing.** Every release becomes a gamble. - **Built by a design team with no consumers.** A system nobody adopted is a cost with no benefit. ## Key takeaways - Treat it as architecture: it is how a11y, theming and consistency are solved once rather than per team. - Two token layers — primitive values, semantic aliases — and components only ever touch the semantic layer. - Compound components plus variants, with a documented escape hatch, is the API shape that survives. - Take behaviour from a headless library; own only appearance. - Semver, codemods, visual regression tests, and usage data are what let it evolve. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How do you roll out a breaking change to 200 components?"** — Deprecate with dev warnings, ship a codemod, track usage, then remove a version later. - **"A team says it doesn't do what they need."** — That is an API gap, not a discipline problem. Give them a lower-level primitive and take the pull request. - **"How do you support white-labelling?"** — Swap the semantic token layer per tenant. It works only if no component ever references a primitive.

learnings.title: Build and deploy topology
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
How code becomes bytes on a user's device is part of the design, and it is where two of the most common production outages live: a cached shell that never updates, and a deploy that breaks every open tab. ## The chunking strategy Chunk boundaries decide how much a user re-downloads after a deploy. | Chunk | Contains | Changes | | --- | --- | --- | | `react.[hash].js` | Framework | Once a quarter | | `vendor.[hash].js` | Other dependencies | Monthly | | `shared.[hash].js` | Your shared UI and utils | Weekly | | `route-feed.[hash].js` | One route | Daily | | `heavy-chart.[hash].js` | A large lazy dependency | Rarely | **Split by change frequency, not by folder.** If your framework and your feature code share a chunk, every deploy invalidates the framework for every user. Separating them means a typical deploy re-downloads 20 kB instead of 700 kB. ```javascript // Route-level splitting is the highest-value split, and almost free. const Feed = lazy(() => import('./routes/Feed')); const Settings = lazy(() => import('./routes/Settings')); // Then component-level for genuinely heavy, rarely used dependencies. const ChartPanel = lazy(() => import('./ChartPanel')); // pulls in ~180 kB ``` ## The caching rule that prevents the worst outage ``` /index.html Cache-Control: no-cache ← always revalidated /assets/app.8f3a2b.js Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable ``` **Hash the assets, never cache the HTML.** The HTML is the manifest that points at the hashed assets; if it is cached, your deploy reaches nobody — and you cannot push a fix, because the fix is also behind the cached HTML. This is the single most common self-inflicted frontend outage. ## Deploy strategies ```mermaid flowchart LR B["Build once"] --> S["Upload assets
keep the old ones"] S --> C["Canary: 1% of traffic"] C -->|"vitals + errors OK"| R["Ramp 10% → 50% → 100%"] C -->|"regression"| K["Roll back the HTML"] ``` - **Upload assets before switching the HTML**, and **keep the previous version's assets live**. A user mid-session is still requesting chunks from the old build; deleting them turns your deploy into their crash. - **Roll back by pointing the HTML at the previous manifest**, not by rebuilding. Rebuilding takes minutes; a pointer swap takes seconds. - **Canary on vitals and error rate, not just on 500s.** A deploy that doubles LCP is an incident. ## The stale-tab problem A user has a tab open. You deploy. Their next lazy chunk request 404s because that hash no longer exists — a blank screen, a cryptic error, and the user's work gone. Two mitigations, and you want both: ```javascript // 1. Keep old assets. Storage is cheap; a broken session is not. // Retain at least the last 3 builds. // 2. Detect the new version and prompt, rather than reloading under them. const res = await fetch('/version.json', { cache: 'no-store' }); const { build } = await res.json(); if (build !== __BUILD_SHA__) { showToast('A new version is available', { action: 'Reload', onAction: () => location.reload() }); } ``` Never force-reload a user who is mid-form. Offer it. ## Environments and configuration Build once, promote the same artefact. Rebuilding per environment means staging never tested what production runs. ```javascript // Runtime config, fetched — not baked in at build time. // Same bundle in staging and production; only this response differs. const config = await fetch('/config.json').then((r) => r.json()); ``` Anything baked into the bundle at build time forces a rebuild per environment and per config change. Only truly static things — the build SHA, the framework mode — belong there. ## The budget that stops the drift ```javascript // A size check in CI that fails the build, not a report nobody reads. { "bundlesize": [ { "path": "dist/assets/index.*.js", "maxSize": "170 kB" }, { "path": "dist/assets/vendor.*.js", "maxSize": "120 kB" } ] } ``` > "I'd put a hard size budget in CI. Bundles don't regress in one bad PR — they grow 4 kB at a time, and without something that fails, nobody is ever the person who broke it." ## Common mistakes - **Caching the HTML.** Your deploy never lands and you cannot ship the fix. - **Deleting the previous build's assets.** Every open session breaks. - **Rebuilding per environment.** Staging did not test production's artefact. - **Splitting by folder instead of by change frequency.** Every deploy invalidates everything. - **Force-reloading on a new version.** You just deleted someone's half-written form. - **A budget that only warns.** It will be ignored, every time. ## Key takeaways - Chunk by change frequency so a deploy invalidates as little as possible. - Hash assets and cache them forever; never cache the HTML. - Keep the last few builds live so open sessions survive a deploy. - Build one artefact and promote it; fetch environment config at runtime. - Canary on vitals and errors, and roll back by swapping the manifest pointer. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How do you roll back in under a minute?"** — Point the HTML at the previous manifest. The assets are already there because you never deleted them. - **"A user's tab has been open for six hours."** — Old chunks are still served, and a version check offers a reload rather than forcing one. - **"How do you stop the bundle growing?"** — A hard CI budget plus a per-PR size diff comment, so the cost is visible at review time.

learnings.title: Multi-tenancy, theming and white-labelling
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
"Can it be rebranded per customer?" turns out to be an architectural question, not a styling one — and the answer is decided by choices you make long before anyone asks.

## The levels

| Level | What varies | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1 — Theming** | Colours, fonts, logo, radius | Semantic token swap at runtime |
| **2 — Branding** | The above plus copy, imagery, domain | Tokens + a content layer |
| **3 — Configuration** | Which features exist, which fields show | Feature flags + a config-driven UI |
| **4 — Customisation** | Custom layouts, custom fields, custom workflows | A schema-driven renderer |
| **5 — Custom code** | Per-tenant components | Plugin architecture — very expensive |

Most products need 1–3 and accidentally build toward 5. Naming the level you are designing for is the first move.

## Level 1–2: tokens, resolved at runtime

```css
/* One stylesheet ships. The values arrive per tenant. */
:root {
  --color-brand: #2563eb;
  --color-brand-fg: #ffffff;
  --font-display: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif;
  --radius-control: 6px;
}
```

```javascript
// Applied before first paint, so there is no flash of the default brand.
const tenant = await fetch(`/api/tenants/${host}/theme`).then((r) => r.json());
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(tenant.tokens)) {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty(`--${key}`, value);
}
```

Two rules make this work, and both are decided early:

1. **No component may reference a raw value** — only semantic tokens. One `#2563eb` inside a component is a component that cannot be re-themed.
2. **Resolve the theme before first paint.** Server-render the token block into the HTML, or inline a tiny blocking script. Otherwise every tenant sees your default brand flash first, which is exactly what they are paying you not to happen.

### Contrast is a correctness problem

A tenant picks a pale yellow brand colour. Your white-on-brand button is now unreadable and you have shipped an accessibility failure to one customer.

```javascript
// Derive the foreground rather than letting the tenant choose it.
const fg = contrastRatio(brand, '#fff') >= 4.5 ? '#fff' : '#111';
```

Validate tenant tokens at the point they are set, and reject or auto-correct combinations that fail AA. This is not gold-plating; it is the difference between a theming feature and a per-tenant bug generator.

## Level 3: configuration

```javascript
// The tenant's capability set, resolved once and read everywhere.
const { features, fields } = useTenantConfig();

{features.exportCsv && <ExportButton />}
{fields.filter((f) => f.visible).map((f) => <Field key={f.id} {...f} />)}
```

The discipline that keeps this maintainable: **the default is always "on" or always "off", consistently, and every flag has an owner and an expiry.** Flags without expiry dates are how a codebase acquires forty permanent branches nobody dares delete.

## Isolation — the part that is a security question

| Concern | The requirement |
| --- | --- |
| **Data** | The server enforces the tenant boundary. A client-side tenant id in a request is a suggestion, not a control. |
| **Cache keys** | Every cache key includes the tenant. Otherwise tenant A's data is served to tenant B — and that is a reportable breach. |
| **Storage** | `localStorage` and IndexedDB are per-origin, not per-tenant. On a shared domain, namespace every key by tenant and clear on switch. |
| **CDN** | Never cache a tenant-specific response publicly. `Vary` on the tenant, or keep it private. |
| **Error tracking** | Tag by tenant so you can tell "broken for everyone" from "broken for one customer". |

> "The riskiest part isn't the theming, it's the cache keys. If the tenant isn't in the key — in React Query, in the service worker, in the CDN — you will eventually serve one customer's data to another. I'd make the tenant part of the key by construction, not by convention."

## Routing per tenant

| Shape | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subdomain | `acme.app.com` | Clean isolation; wildcard TLS; separate storage origins **(the safest)** |
| Path | `app.com/acme` | Simplest; shared origin means shared storage — namespace carefully |
| Custom domain | `portal.acme.com` | What enterprise customers actually want; you now own certificate provisioning |

## Common mistakes

- **Hard-coded values in components.** Themability is now a rewrite.
- **Theme applied after hydration.** Every tenant sees your brand first.
- **Letting tenants pick both foreground and background.** You have outsourced your contrast compliance.
- **Tenant id missing from a cache key.** Cross-tenant data leak.
- **Flags with no expiry.** Permanent branching, untestable combinations.
- **Trusting a client-supplied tenant id.** The server must enforce it.

## Key takeaways

- Decide the level: token theming, branding, configuration, schema-driven, or plugins.
- Semantic tokens only, resolved before first paint.
- Derive foreground colours and validate contrast — tenant input is untrusted design input.
- Tenant identity belongs in every cache key, everywhere, or you will leak data across tenants.
- The server enforces the tenant boundary; the client only displays it.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"A tenant wants a different layout on one page."** — That is level 4. Either a schema-driven renderer or a documented slot in that page — not a per-tenant branch in the component.
- **"How do you prevent one tenant's data reaching another?"** — Server-side enforcement, plus the tenant in every cache key at every layer. Say all the layers.
- **"How do you test 40 tenants?"** — Test the mechanism against a few representative token sets, plus automated contrast validation on every tenant's configuration.

learnings.title: Observability — knowing it broke before the user tells you
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Backends get observability by default: logs, metrics, traces, all on machines you own. The frontend runs on devices you will never see, and unless you deliberately build a way to hear from them, your only monitoring is a support ticket.

Naming this in a design round is a cheap, reliable senior signal.

## The four signals

| Signal | Answers | Tools |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **RUM** | Is it fast for real people? | `web-vitals` → your own endpoint, CrUX, SpeedCurve |
| **Errors** | Is it broken, and where? | Sentry, Rollbar, Bugsnag |
| **Product analytics** | Did they succeed at the task? | Amplitude, PostHog, Mixpanel |
| **Session replay** | *Why* did it break? | Sentry Replay, FullStory, LogRocket |

You need all four because each answers a question the others cannot. Vitals say the page was fast; errors say nothing threw; and the user still could not check out.

## Errors, made actionable

Raw error counts are noise. Three things turn them into something you can act on:

```javascript
Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN,
  release: __BUILD_SHA__,        // 1. which deploy introduced it
  environment: __ENV__,
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0, // replay every session that errored
  beforeSend(event) {
    // 2. drop the noise that is not yours
    if (event.exception?.values?.[0]?.value?.includes('ResizeObserver loop')) return null;
    if (isBrowserExtensionFrame(event)) return null;
    return event;
  },
});

// 3. who and where — without shipping personal data
Sentry.setUser({ id: user.id });          // an id, never an email
Sentry.setTag('tenant', tenant.id);
Sentry.setTag('route', location.pathname);
```

**Source maps are the difference between usable and useless.** Upload them at build time and do not serve them publicly — an error in `a.min.js:1:48291` tells you nothing.

### Error boundaries decide the blast radius

```javascript
// One boundary per major region. A crashed chart should not
// take the navigation with it.
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<ChartFailed onRetry={refetch} />}>
  <RevenueChart />
</ErrorBoundary>
```

Where you place boundaries is an architectural decision: it determines whether a bug degrades one panel or blanks the page. Note that boundaries do **not** catch errors in event handlers, in async code, or during SSR — those need `window.onerror`, `unhandledrejection`, and server-side handling respectively.

## Tracing across the boundary

The highest-value and least-implemented piece. Propagate a trace id from the browser into the backend so one user's slow request is one timeline, not two disconnected investigations:

```javascript
const traceId = crypto.randomUUID();
fetch('/api/feed', { headers: { 'traceparent': `00-${traceId}-${spanId}-01` } });
```

> "I'd propagate W3C trace context from the client. Without it, 'the feed is slow for this customer' is two separate investigations that never meet in the middle."

## Sampling and volume

You cannot send everything from every session; the beacon traffic becomes its own problem.

| Data | Sample |
| --- | --- |
| Web vitals | 100% — they are tiny and you need the p75 |
| Errors | 100%, with aggressive deduplication server-side |
| Traces | 1–10%, plus 100% of anything that errored |
| Session replay | ~1% baseline, 100% on error |
| Custom events | 100% for funnel steps, sample the chatter |

Always use `navigator.sendBeacon` for telemetry on unload — `fetch` is routinely cancelled when the page goes away, which silently biases your data toward sessions that did not leave.

## Privacy is a design constraint

- **No PII in error payloads.** User ids, never emails or names. Scrub URLs with tokens in them.
- **Mask inputs in session replay by default**, and opt specific fields *in*, never out.
- **Telemetry is usually "non-essential"** under GDPR, so it waits for consent — which means it cannot be on your critical path anyway.
- **Data residency** may dictate which vendor and region you may use at all.

## Alerting on what users feel

Alert on symptoms, not causes:

| Alert | Threshold |
| --- | --- |
| JS error rate | > 2× the 7-day baseline for 10 min |
| p75 LCP | > 2.5 s on a key route for 15 min |
| API failure rate | > 1% on a critical endpoint |
| Checkout funnel drop | > 20% below the same hour last week |

That last one catches the class of bug nothing else does: **no errors, good vitals, and the button silently does nothing.**

## Common mistakes

- **Errors with no release tag.** You cannot tell which deploy caused it.
- **No source maps.** Minified stack traces are unreadable.
- **One error boundary at the root.** Any bug blanks the whole app.
- **Sending PII to a third party.** A compliance incident with your name on it.
- **`fetch` for unload beacons.** Cancelled, and your data quietly skews.
- **Vitals without funnels.** Fast and broken looks healthy on every dashboard.

## Key takeaways

- Four signals — RUM, errors, analytics, replay — because each answers a different question.
- Tag every event with release, route and tenant, or it is not actionable.
- Error boundaries per region decide the blast radius of a bug.
- Propagate W3C trace context so client and server slowness is one timeline.
- Alert on user-visible symptoms, including funnel drops that throw no errors.
- `sendBeacon`, never `fetch`, for anything sent on unload.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you know a deploy made things worse?"** — Release-tagged vitals and error rates, compared against the previous release on the same routes, during the canary.
- **"A user says it's broken and you can't reproduce it."** — Session replay filtered to their user id, plus the trace id from their request.
- **"How much does this cost?"** — Sampling is the lever: 100% vitals and errors, 1–10% traces, 1% replay with 100% on error.
